title: He Won the World Cup Six Months Ago. He Lost the Captaincy Last Week. His First Words Were About Someone Else.
excerpt: Suryakumar Yadav's reaction to losing the India T20I captaincy was a masterclass in grace — and a reminder that three consecutive Mumbai captains now lead India's shortest format.
body:
In the hours after the Board of Control for Cricket in India announced that Shreyas Iyer would replace him as India's T20I captain, Suryakumar Yadav did something that captains who lose their crowns almost never do.

He celebrated the man who took it.

On his Instagram story, Suryakumar posted a photograph of the Indian team — the team that would travel to Ireland and England without him — and wrote a single line: "Wishing this highly skilled group all the best for the challenges ahead."

No bitterness. No cryptic subtweets. No "sources close to the player say he is disappointed." Just a man making room.

Later that day, at a T20 Mumbai League match between Triumph Knights MNE and SoBo Mumbai Falcons, the two men found themselves on opposite sides of the field. Before the toss, Suryakumar and Iyer shared a long hug — the kind that comes from fifteen years of sharing nets, dressing rooms, and the particular grind of Mumbai cricket.

"Very, very, very happy for Shreyas as he's getting to lead the T20 Indian team," Suryakumar said at the toss, smiling broadly. "We played a lot of cricket together in Bombay. The most important thing, what I felt, is that three back-to-back Mumbai captains are going to lead T20s for India. I think it's a very proud moment, and everyone needs to celebrate that."

Three captains. Two World Cup trophies between them. One city.

Rohit Sharma led India to the 2024 T20 World Cup title in Barbados. Suryakumar took over and defended it in 2026. Now Shreyas Iyer inherits the armband. All three emerged from the same Mumbai cricket ecosystem — the same khadoos culture of earning your place, the same Wankhede Stadium that has produced more international cricketers than most countries.

The decision was not without controversy. Chief selector Ajit Agarkar acknowledged the difficulty publicly: "With regards to Surya, obviously, it's a tough one, having just won the World Cup. Someone who's led you to the World Cup, it's not the easiest thing to try and change."

For NRIs who followed Suryakumar's improbable rise — from being repeatedly overlooked for India selection despite domestic dominance, to becoming arguably the most innovative T20 batter in the world — the captaincy change stings. He was dropped from the squad entirely for the Ireland, England, and Asian Games assignments.

But Suryakumar, characteristically, refused to make the story about himself. He has been left out of India squads before. He spent years watching less talented players get picked ahead of him. And each time, he responded the same way: he scored runs, he waited, and when the door opened, he walked through it so emphatically that it could never be shut again.

Rohit Sharma, the man who preceded both of them, offered his own endorsement of Iyer: "You have to really earn it. Captaincy is something that you have to earn and earn the respect of people around you. Looking at how he has captained in the last few years for his franchise, he's going to have a good time as well."

Iyer arrives fresh off an IPL 2026 season where he scored 498 runs for Punjab Kings. Tilak Varma, another young Mumbai product, has been named vice-captain. The conveyor belt shows no signs of slowing.

For diaspora cricket fans scattered across North America, the UK, and the Gulf, the Mumbai captaincy pipeline is a quietly extraordinary thing. In a sport that has historically been dominated by the northern and eastern heartlands — Delhi, Kolkata, Hyderabad — the financial capital has spent the last three years producing India's T20 leaders as reliably as it produces investment bankers.

Suryakumar Yadav is 35. He has not retired. He has not said this is the end. And if the pattern of his career holds, the next chapter will begin with everyone counting him out — and end with everyone wondering how they ever did.
